items.back: For $p∈E'$, $\lim_{x→p}f(x)=q$ if for every $ε>0$ there is $δ>0$ with $d_{Y}(f(x),q)<ε$ whenever $x∈E$ and $0<d_{X}(x,p)<δ$.
For every $ε>0$ there is $δ>0$ with $d_{Y}(f(x),f(p))<ε$ whenever $x∈E$, $d_{X}(x,p)<δ$. Note $p$ must be in $E$, and need not be a limit point.
$|f(x)|≤M$ for all $x$.
For every $ε>0$ there is one $δ>0$ that works for all $p,q$: $d_{X}(p,q)<δ ⇒ d_{Y}(f(p),f(q))<ε$.
$f(x+)=q$ if $f(t_{n})→q$ for every sequence $t_{n}↓x$ with $t_{n}>x$; similarly $f(x−)$.

items.front: Discontinuities of the first and second kind
items.back: First kind (simple): $f(x+)$ and $f(x−)$ both exist but $f$ is not continuous at $x$. Second kind: otherwise.
Increasing if $x<y ⇒ f(x)≤f(y)$.
Stated with neighborhoods $(c,+∞)$ of $+∞$ so the definition of 4.1 carries over.
$\lim_{x→p}f(x)=q$ iff $f(p_{n})→q$ for every sequence $p_{n}$ in $E$ with $p_{n}≠p$, $p_{n}→p$.
items.note: Best tool for showing a limit does not exist: find two sequences with different limits.

items.back: Sums, products and quotients of limits behave as expected.
If $p∈E$ is a limit point of $E$, $f$ is continuous at $p$ iff $\lim_{x→p}f(x)=f(p)$. At isolated points every $f$ is continuous.
If $f$ is continuous at $p$ and $g$ at $f(p)$, then $g∘f$ is continuous at $p$.
$f:X→Y$ is continuous iff $f^{−1}(V)$ is open for every open $V⊂Y$ (equivalently, preimages of closed sets are closed).
items.note: Makes “$\{x: f(x)>0\}$ is open” a one-liner.

items.back: If $X$ is compact and $f$ continuous, $f(X)$ is compact.
A continuous real function on a compact space attains its max and min.
A continuous bijection from a compact space has a continuous inverse.
A continuous map on a compact metric space is uniformly continuous.

If $E⊂ℝ$ is not compact, there is a continuous function on $E$ that is unbounded, and one that is bounded but has no maximum. If $E$ is also bounded, there is a continuous function on $E$ that is not uniformly continuous.
If $E$ is connected and $f$ continuous, $f(E)$ is connected.
If $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and $c$ is between $f(a)$ and $f(b)$, then $f(x)=c$ for some $x∈(a,b)$.
If $f$ increases on $(a,b)$, then $f(x−)=\sup_{t<x}f(t) ≤ f(x) ≤ \inf_{t>x}f(t)=f(x+)$.
A monotone function has at most countably many discontinuities, all of the first kind.
items.note: Rudin 4.31 shows the set can still be dense.

items.front: Extra tools from the other books
items.back: Lipschitz ⇒ uniformly continuous (B 5.4.5). Uniformly continuous maps send Cauchy sequences to Cauchy sequences (B 5.4.7). $f$ is uniformly continuous on $(a,b)$ iff it extends continuously to $[a,b]$ (B 5.4.8). The set of discontinuities of any $f:ℝ→ℝ$ is an $F_{σ}$ set (A 4.6.6).

items.prompt: Prove: Extreme value theorem.
items.modelProof: $f(X)$ is compact (4.14), so closed and bounded in $ℝ$. Its sup $M$ exists and lies in the closure (2.28), which is $f(X)$ itself. So $M=f(p)$ for some $p$.

items.prompt: Prove: Compact ⇒ uniformly continuous (sequence version).
items.modelProof: If not, there are $ε>0$ and $p_{n},q_{n}$ with $d(p_{n},q_{n})<1/n$ but $d(f(p_{n}),f(q_{n}))≥ε$. By compactness $p_{n_{k}}→p$, so $q_{n_{k}}→p$ too. Continuity at $p$ forces $d(f(p_{n_{k}}),f(q_{n_{k}}))→0$, a contradiction. (Rudin uses an open-cover argument; A 4.4.7 uses this one.)

items.prompt: Prove: IVT by a sup argument.
items.modelProof: Say $f(a)<c<f(b)$. Let $s=\sup\{x∈[a,b]: f(x)<c\}$. If $f(s)<c$, continuity puts points just right of $s$ in the set; if $f(s)>c$, a whole interval left of $s$ is outside the set. Both contradict the definition of $s$, so $f(s)=c$. (Rudin instead uses connectedness, 4.22.)

items.prompt: Prove: Preimage characterization.
items.modelProof: ($⇒$) If $V$ is open and $f(p)∈V$, pick $ε$ with $N_{ε}(f(p))⊂V$ and the matching $δ$; then $N_{δ}(p)⊂f^{−1}(V)$. ($⇐$) Apply the hypothesis to $V=N_{ε}(f(p))$; $p$ is an interior point of $f^{−1}(V)$, which gives $δ$.

items.prompt: Prove: Monotone discontinuities are countable.
items.modelProof: At each discontinuity $x$ of increasing $f$, $f(x−)<f(x+)$; choose a rational $r(x)$ strictly between them. Different $x$ give disjoint intervals, so $x↦r(x)$ is one-to-one into $ℚ$.

items.prompt: Prove with ε–δ that $f(x)=\sqrt x$ is continuous at every $c>0$.
Prove $1/x$ is uniformly continuous on $[1,∞)$ but not on $(0,1)$.
items.modelProof: On $[1,∞)$, $xy≥1$, so $δ=ε$ works (Lipschitz). On $(0,1)$, $x_{n}=1/n$ and $y_{n}=1/(n+1)$ get arbitrarily close while $|1/x_{n}−1/y_{n}|=1$.

items.prompt: If $f:X→Y$ is continuous, prove $f(\bar E)⊂\overline{f(E)}$. Give an example where the inclusion is strict.
items.hint: Take $p∈\bar E$ and a sequence in $E$ converging to it, or use 4.8.
items.modelProof: $f^{−1}(\overline{f(E)})$ is closed and contains $E$, so it contains $\bar E$. Strict: $f=\arctan$, $E=ℝ$: $f(\bar E)=(−π/2,π/2)$ but its closure adds $±π/2$.

items.prompt: If $f$ is a continuous real function on a metric space $X$, prove $Z(f)=\{p: f(p)=0\}$ is closed.
Prove every real polynomial of odd degree has a real root.
items.hint: Look at the sign for large $|x|$.
items.modelProof: If the leading coefficient is positive, $p(x)→+∞$ as $x→+∞$ and $→−∞$ as $x→−∞$. Pick $a,b$ with $p(a)<0<p(b)$ and apply the IVT.

items.prompt: Let $f(x)=x\sin(1/x)$ for $x≠0$ and $f(0)=0$. Prove $f$ is uniformly continuous on $[−1,1]$.
items.modelProof: Away from 0 it is a composition of continuous functions. At 0, $|f(x)|≤|x|$, so take $δ=ε$. $[−1,1]$ is compact, so 4.19 gives uniform continuity.

items.prompt: If $f$ is continuous and bounded on $(0,1)$, then $f$ is uniformly continuous.
If $f$ is uniformly continuous on $(0,1)$, then $f$ is bounded.
items.explanation: It extends continuously to $[0,1]$ (B 5.4.8), which is compact.

items.prompt: The continuous image of an open set is open.
The preimage of a compact set under a continuous map is compact.
items.explanation: A constant map $ℝ→ℝ$: the preimage of $\{0\}$ is $ℝ$.

items.prompt: If $f$ and $g$ are both discontinuous at $c$, so is $f+g$.
If $|f|$ is continuous, then $f$ is continuous.
A continuous one-to-one $f:[a,b]→ℝ$ is strictly monotone.
items.explanation: If not, three points $x<y<z$ have $f(y)$ above (or below) both $f(x)$ and $f(z)$; IVT then gives a repeated value.

items.prompt: Every continuous $f:[0,1]→[0,1]$ has a fixed point.
If $f:ℝ→ℝ$ is continuous and $f(q)=0$ for every rational $q$, then $f≡0$.
items.explanation: Each real is a limit of rationals; use the sequential criterion (or: the zero set is closed and dense).

lines: Since $ε$ was arbitrary, $x^{2}$ is uniformly continuous on $ℝ$.
items.explanation: $δ$ depends on $x$. That proves continuity at each point, not uniform continuity. The claim is false: $x_{n}=n$, $y_{n}=n+1/n$ are close but $|x_{n}^{2}−y_{n}^{2}|>2$.

items.claim: Every continuous $f$ on $(0,1]$ attains a maximum.
lines: By the extreme value theorem, a continuous function on a bounded set attains its maximum.
items.explanation: EVT needs a compact domain, and $(0,1]$ is not closed. $f(x)=−x$ has sup 0, never attained.

lines: The sequential criterion: $f$ is continuous at 0 if $f(x_{n})→f(0)$ whenever $x_{n}→0$.
items.explanation: The criterion requires every sequence tending to 0, not one. $f=1_{Q}$ has $f(1/n)=1=f(0)$ but is discontinuous at 0.

items.name: Dirichlet function $1_{Q}$
items.details: Discontinuous everywhere, every discontinuity of the second kind (A §4.1).

items.name: Thomae's function
items.details: $f(p/q)=1/q$ in lowest terms, $f=0$ on irrationals. Continuous exactly at the irrationals.

items.name: $1/x$ on $(0,1)$
items.details: Continuous, unbounded, not uniformly continuous. $x^{2}$ on $ℝ$: continuous, not uniformly continuous.

items.name: $\sin(1/x)$ with $f(0)=0$
items.details: Has the intermediate value property but is not continuous at 0; discontinuity of the second kind.

items.name: $t↦(\cos t,\sin t)$ on $[0,2π)$
items.details: Continuous bijection onto the circle whose inverse is not continuous at $(1,0)$ (Rudin 4.21).

items.name: $f(x)=Σ_{x_{n}<x}2^{−n}$ for an enumeration $(x_{n})$ of $ℚ$
items.details: Increasing, with a jump at every rational (Rudin 4.31).
